title: From tap to server: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP
dek: Between a customer tapping a restaurant and the menu appearing, the phone finds the server, opens a connection, secures it and asks. Each step costs a round trip, and round trips, not bandwidth, decide how fast most apps feel. Here is what happens on the wire, and how to choose a way to push live updates.

items: Before the first byte of a menu arrives, the phone finds the server (DNS), opens a connection (TCP), secures it (TLS) and sends the request (HTTP): up to four round trips.
Round trips, not bandwidth, decide how fast most API calls feel. Reuse connections, keep servers close to users, and make fewer, bigger requests.
For live updates, choose between polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets by how often the data changes and which way it flows.

body.x: Four round trips before the first byte

body.cap: On a fresh connection the phone pays for DNS, TCP and TLS before it can even ask for the menu. That is why apps keep connections open and reuse them: every later request costs one round trip.

items: DNS turns api.zotato.in into an IP address. The answer is cached by the phone and the resolver for the record's time to live, so later lookups are usually free.
TCP opens a reliable, ordered connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, then data can flow. Lost packets are resent and the receiver gets bytes in order.
TLS agrees encryption keys and proves the server is really api.zotato.in, using its certificate. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip; resuming an earlier session can need none.
HTTP finally sends the request and gets the response. Everything before it was overhead.

body.x: How long is a round trip? Inside one data centre, well under a millisecond. Between Mumbai and Delhi over fibre, around 25 to 35 ms. A 4G phone adds tens of milliseconds of its own, and India to the US east coast is about 200 ms. Four of those before the first byte is why the first screen of an app is always the slowest.

items: Use TCP when every byte must arrive, in order: API calls, payments, file uploads, database traffic.
Use UDP when late data is worthless (live voice, video calls, game state) or when the protocol on top handles loss itself, as DNS and QUIC do.
TCP's guarantee has a cost: if one packet is lost, everything after it waits until it is resent, even data for other requests. This is called head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/1.1 handles one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections to load a page.
HTTP/2 carries many requests at once over one TCP connection and compresses headers. One lost packet still stalls all of them, because TCP delivers in order.

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP. Each request is its own stream, so a lost packet only delays its own request; setup takes one round trip including encryption; and a connection survives the phone switching from Wi-Fi to 4G.
Reuse connections: keep-alive from the app, and connection pools between your own services. A new TLS connection per call is the most common hidden cost.
Put servers and a CDN near your users. For customers in India, a Mumbai region saves 150 ms or more on every round trip compared with a US one.
Make fewer round trips: one call that returns the whole restaurant page beats five calls in a row, and calls that don't depend on each other should run in parallel.
Send fewer bytes: compress responses, send only the fields the screen needs, and serve resized images.
Put a timeout on every network call. The Timeouts concept explains why.

body.cap: The same three location updates delivered four ways. Polling is simple but wasteful and late; the other three deliver each update as it happens, at the cost of keeping something open on the server for every waiting user.

body.label: Choosing a way to push updates
head: Method
How it works
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Polling
The app asks every few seconds
Rare changes; simplest to build
Mostly empty requests; news is late by up to one interval
Long polling
The server holds the request until there is news (or about 30 s), then the app asks again
Near-live updates over plain HTTP
One held request per waiting user
Server-sent events
One HTTP response stays open; the server writes events into it
One-way updates: order status, rider location, scores
Server to app only; one open connection per user
WebSocket
One connection upgraded to two-way messages
Chat, live collaboration, anything both sides send often
Connection servers to run and scale; reconnects and missed messages to handle

body.x: Order tracking at Zotato needs updates from the server only, so server-sent events are enough; the rider chat sends messages both ways, so it uses a WebSocket. Either way, the open connections live on dedicated connection servers, and a message bus tells the right one which user to notify (see the Chat app problem).
Load balancers work at different layers

A layer 4 load balancer spreads TCP connections without reading them: fast and simple, but it can't route by URL. A layer 7 load balancer reads HTTP: it can send /api to one group of servers and /images to another, end TLS for them, and retry a failed request elsewhere. The Load balancers component covers both.

items: When latency matters, count round trips: a new connection costs three or four before any work is done.
Say where servers sit relative to users, and what a CDN serves from nearby.
Pick the live-update method by direction and frequency: server-sent events for one-way updates, WebSockets for two-way, polling only when updates are rare.
Name HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 if many small requests or flaky mobile networks matter, and TCP versus UDP if the question involves voice or video.

body.label: Go deeper: why a new connection is slow even after the handshakes

body.x: A new TCP connection doesn't know how much the network can carry, so it starts by sending only about ten packets (around 14 KB) and roughly doubles that every round trip while nothing is lost. A 100 KB response on a brand-new connection therefore needs several extra round trips; on a connection that has been in use for a while it can arrive in one. This 'slow start' is another reason to keep connections open and to keep the first screen's responses small.
